video_title: The World After the Blue Wave - What Changes for Ukraine, Iran, Israel & U.S. Defence?
gist: Perun analyzes the defense and strategic implications of the Democratic sweep of both chambers in the 2026 US midterms: a smaller-than-requested defense budget nearer $1T, likely death of the nuclear-powered battleships, a scaled-back Golden Dome, and packaging fights that delay even popular munitions funding. Internationally Israel is the clearest loser, Iran is a 'we'll see' with possible near-term escalation risk, and Ukraine and NATO allies gain mostly from fewer bad surprises rather than new aid.

insights.claim: Democrats won control of both chambers in the 2026 US midterms, reaching at least 54 Senate seats (possibly 55-56) versus the 52 considered needed for safe control, up from 47.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A wave of this size locks in Senate seats for six years, shaping defense appropriations through at least 2030.
insights.quote: As at time of recording, they've already got at least 54.

insights.claim: Because Senate terms are six years, wave gains such as Kansas's first Democratic senator since 1932 are baked in for more than half a decade regardless of 2028 or 2030 swings.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Policy durability: defense budget politics shift structurally, not for a single cycle.

insights.claim: Texas, an economy comparable to Italy's, now has a Democratic governor, which changes state-level leverage over firms headquartered there such as SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: State-level political shifts can create new regulatory/political pressure points on major defense-adjacent contractors.

insights.claim: The Democratic Senate majority falls short of the 60-vote filibuster threshold and far short of the two-thirds needed to override vetoes or convict in impeachment, so Congress gains blocking and agenda power rather than total budgetary control.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect gridlock and delay rather than decisive new policy; positions should price obstruction, not reversal.

insights.claim: Every White House nominee needing Senate confirmation will now require some Democratic votes, while Congress's subpoena and impeachment powers make officials like Secretary Hegseth (originally confirmed 51-50 via tie-break) vulnerable to investigations and pressured resignations.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Leadership churn and oversight at the Pentagon can disrupt program priorities and procurement direction.
insights.quote: Someone like Secretary Hegseth for example might be in a bit of a vulnerable position.

insights.claim: The White House's record $1.5 trillion defense request (about $1.15T regular appropriations plus about $350B via reconciliation, plus a roughly $90B Iran war supplemental) had not cleared Congress even under Republican control, as the GOP Senate leader reportedly lacked votes for reconciliation.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Headline topline was never secure; defense primes' growth expectations tied to $1.5T were already at risk.

insights.claim: The ranking Democrat on House Armed Services has signaled opposition to a defense budget above $1 trillion, implying the final budget will come in significantly smaller than requested and closer to recent budgets.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect cuts to wish-list items and a topline nearer $1T; elevated but not surge-level spend for contractors.
insights.quote: one that does not require a defense budget in excess of 1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs

insights.claim: Congress shapes procurement at line-item level (e.g., funding two extra Arleigh Burke destroyers when the Pentagon asked for one), while the presidential veto operates only on whole packages, giving the new majority power to set program numbers.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Program-level funding outcomes now depend on Democrat-controlled armed services committees.

insights.claim: Defense spending with parochial bipartisan support, such as shipbuilding (e.g., Mississippi's shipyard), destroyers, amphibs and uncrewed systems, is likely to survive regardless of party control.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Shipbuilders and uncrewed-systems suppliers are relatively insulated from the political swing.

insights.claim: Pentagon can shuffle authorized funds internally, but new initiatives like an autonomous warfare command need specific appropriations to actually be staffed and operate.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: New White House defense initiatives without appropriations may exist on paper only.

insights.claim: Overall, an elevated defense spend versus most of the last decade is still likely, but expensive, politically charged, highly visible programs already opposed by Democrats are in the firing line, with a large gray zone of uncertainty in between.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Framework for sorting defense exposure: bipartisan baseline safe, vanity/visible programs at risk.
insights.quote: Particularly expensive, politically charged, highly visible programs that have already been opposed by Democrats are likely to be in the firing line.

themes.theme: Battleships and Golden Dome on the block

insights.claim: The planned nuclear-powered battleships (BBGN, starting with USS Defiant, at least 15 planned) are probably doomed to death, delay or defunding under a Democratic Congress.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Any contractor value tied to the battleship program should be heavily discounted; funding likely redirects to Arleigh Burkes and other platforms.
insights.quote: Voters probably, for example, just sunk the new nuclear-powered battleships

insights.claim: CBO estimates put the Defiant at north of $20 billion and follow-on ships around $18 billion each, making each roughly 35,000-ton BBGN more expensive than a 100,000-ton Ford-class carrier, with a $275 billion program cost through 2056 cited by Democrats.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Cost-per-ton disparity makes the program the obvious target for cuts.

insights.claim: Democrats called the battleship program an ill-conceived vanity project that would take resources from destroyers, amphibs, carriers and unmanned vessels.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Reallocation from battleships likely benefits destroyer, amphib and unmanned vessel lines.
insights.quote: this program is an ill-conceived vanity project that will have a net negative impact on Navy force design and the American shipbuilding industrial base

insights.claim: The F-47 sixth-generation fighter enjoys more congressional support than the battleship despite its naming issue, because it is seen as something the US military actually needs.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Distinguishes politically branded but needed programs (likely safe) from vanity ones (at risk).

insights.claim: The battleship cancellation would likely occur before steel is cut, limiting sunk costs, and continues a pattern where new Navy concepts are dropped and the Navy goes back to building Arleigh Burkes.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Arleigh Burke production line remains the default beneficiary of Navy program churn.

insights.claim: Golden Dome may be rebranded or scaled back, with ambitious elements like space-based interceptors discarded or delayed, while core air and missile defense such as AMTI satellites, sensors and interceptors likely survive.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Space-based interceptor plays are at higher risk than sensor/AMTI and conventional interceptor suppliers.
insights.quote: in a tighter budgetary environment, you're probably looking at a different kind of dome.

insights.claim: Golden Dome cost estimates diverge enormously: about $185 billion over a decade per the Space Force general managing it versus $1.19 trillion over 20 years per CBO, including 7,800 space-based interceptors with about five-year orbital lifetimes.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Huge cost uncertainty makes the program politically vulnerable and its addressable market highly uncertain.

insights.claim: Missile defense against capable opponents like China or Russia is economically daunting because adding offensive systems is almost always cheaper than adding enough defensive systems, which is why such systems historically target North Korea, Iran or rogue launches.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Cost-exchange logic undermines the case for maximalist national missile defense spending.

insights.claim: Popular items are bundled in unpopular packages: $21B for munition replacements, $2.4B for drones and $4B for AMTI-related systems sit in the Iran-associated funding, which may make them politically toxic and delay them.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Even bipartisan munition and drone funding could slip, delaying contract awards.
insights.quote: So you might end up with some potentially agreeable components in a thoroughly unagreeable package.

insights.claim: Nearly all Golden Dome funding (about $17.5B) sits in the reconciliation request that could theoretically pass by simple majority before January, giving it a short-term survival path despite Democratic opposition.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Watch the lame-duck window: reconciliation passage before January would lock in funding Democrats would otherwise cut.

insights.claim: About a third of the reconciliation request was for the defense industrial base, including over $48B for critical minerals, followed by next-generation technology/autonomy and then munitions such as Patriot, THAAD, SM-3, SM-6, Tomahawk, AMRAAM, JASSM and PrSM.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Critical minerals, autonomy and munitions makers have significant funding contingent on the fate of reconciliation.

insights.claim: Because agreeable and disagreeable line items are clustered together, the new majority will likely push for significant changes, implying fraught negotiations, potential shutdowns and almost certain delays even for popular initiatives like munition production.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect timing risk on defense contract flows in early 2027 even where funding is ultimately agreed.
insights.quote: which means fraught negotiations, potential shutdowns, and almost certain delays.

insights.claim: It is unclear how munitions and spare parts already expended in the Iran war will be replenished if a supplemental fails: absorbed into the regular budget, a smaller supplemental, or not at all.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Replenishment demand for expended munitions is real but its funding vehicle is uncertain.

insights.claim: Israel is the biggest early strategic loser of the election, because it depends heavily on a US relationship that is deteriorating and lacks a written alliance, mutual defense clause or large US basing to give it legal or logistic inertia.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Declining US backing raises Israel's need for domestic defense production and alternative suppliers.
insights.quote: there's a strong argument I'd suggest to give it to Israel

insights.claim: Gallup-type data show falling US favorability toward Israel, and a May 2026 survey found 47% of over-65s but only 18% of 18-29 year olds (28% of young Republicans) favored the Israeli government, signaling a generational as well as partisan breakdown.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Long-term erosion of US political support for Israeli military aid as younger cohorts age into the electorate.

insights.claim: Senate votes to restrict arms shipments to Israel rose from 11 to 27 to 40 by April, per Yair Lapid.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Clear trend toward conditioning or restricting US arms transfers to Israel.
insights.quote: two years ago, 11 senators voted to restrict arms shipments to Israel. Last year, the number rose to 27. By April, it was already 40

insights.claim: Before the election the White House announced it would cut nearly $4 billion a year of military aid to Israel, putting it on Ukraine-style pay-for-weapons rules, and VP Vance listed changing the relationship with Israel as a post-election suggestion.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Israel shifts from grant recipient to paying customer for US weapons, affecting FMS flows and Israeli defense budgets.

insights.claim: Israel remains dependent on foreign supply lines: its air force is overwhelmingly US platforms, submarines are German-built, some munitions would face supply squeezes without US shipments, and it had no analog to the B-2 strikes in Operation Midnight Hammer.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Israel's capability gaps may drive spending on domestic munitions and non-US suppliers.

insights.claim: Unlike Ukraine, which partially pivoted to Europe after US aid stopped, Israel has no clear equivalent geopolitical backup to Washington.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Asymmetric downside for Israel if US support continues eroding.

insights.claim: Iran may read the vote as a repudiation of the war and gain negotiating confidence, but it faces immense damage from the US blockade and a lame-duck president free of midterm concerns, so the outcome is a 'we'll see'.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Middle East risk and oil-related volatility remain unresolved despite anti-war sentiment.

insights.claim: With a third US carrier group en route to CENTCOM and two years until the next election, the window before January when three carriers are in theater may be militarily attractive for renewed escalation, as Bush surged into Iraq after losing the 2006 midterms.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Short-term escalation risk may rise, not fall, after the midterms, with implications for oil and munitions demand.
insights.quote: a swing in the mid-terms doesn't historically mean an end to the freedom of the White House to act.

insights.claim: The election was fought mainly on economy and affordability, with the Middle East war and the correlated jump in fuel costs the war in the electoral crosshairs.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Energy price spikes from Middle East conflict carry measurable political cost, constraining future escalation.

insights.claim: A standalone Ukraine aid package is unlikely to survive a presidential veto, which requires two-thirds in both chambers; more likely is Ukraine becoming a wedge issue with forced votes.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Do not expect a surge of new US Ukraine aid; European funding remains the main source.

insights.claim: Congress is likely to use the 'paper clip' tactic of attaching Ukraine measures to must-pass bills like the NDAA, as already attempted with $750 million of USAI in the Senate FY2027 draft.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Small incremental Ukraine purchases from US industry are more likely via must-pass legislation.

insights.claim: Of about $33.5 billion appropriated for USAI, about 57% had been delivered as of March 2026 and still 57% in August 2026 per the Pentagon Inspector General, suggesting stalled deliveries the new Congress may push.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Roughly $14B of authorized but undelivered funds could flow to US contractors if Congress forces execution.

insights.claim: An October YouGov poll found US voters sympathize with Ukraine over Russia by 22 to 1, making a veto seen as protecting Moscow politically costly.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Political cost constrains overtly pro-Russia White House moves like sanctions relief.

insights.claim: The US retains major levers over Ukraine even without aid, including sanctions, transfer permits, munition prioritization and control of Starlink/Starshield via speed limits and geofencing; future Starshield disruptions may now face congressional investigation.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: SpaceX's role in Ukraine becomes a political/oversight risk area.

insights.claim: Ukraine was left almost entirely dependent on European assistance after US aid halted, making events like France's 2027 election far more consequential for its war effort.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: European elections in 2027 are the next key political risk for Ukraine support and European defense budgets.

insights.claim: Overall the midterms are probably about the best outcome Ukraine could hope for: less about new aid and more about making pro-Russian White House moves, like Russian diesel imports, sanctions relief or energy-asset deals tied to Witkoff and Kushner, more costly; Kyiv is cautiously optimistic and Moscow frustrated.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Reduced tail risk of US-brokered pro-Russia settlement or sanctions relief.
insights.quote: From a Ukrainian perspective, the change is less about what is now likely to happen as what is now less likely to happen.

insights.claim: A Democratic Congress is unlikely to dismantle the tariff regime because reclaiming delegated tariff powers requires legislation subject to veto, but it may make new trade escalations more politically painful.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Existing tariffs likely persist; new escalation risk modestly reduced.

insights.claim: The 2026 NDAA barred permanent reductions of US troops in Europe below 75,000, and allies may seek more such guardrails, but Congress cannot force the White House to actually defend anyone under Article 5.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Congressional guardrails limit drawdowns but not deterrence credibility, sustaining allied self-reliance spending.
insights.quote: it can defend the defense treaties, but it can't force the White House to actually defend anyone because of them.

insights.claim: Allied confidence in the White House is dismal, with doubters outnumbering confident respondents about 3 to 1 in the UK, 2 to 1 in Poland and over 4 to 1 in Germany per the Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Persistent trust deficit underpins sustained European defense spending.

insights.claim: European rearmament is unlikely to slow because of the change in Congress, as pressures around the transatlantic relationship, Russia-Ukraine and NATO's spending agreements remain.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: European defense industry demand remains structurally supported regardless of US midterms.
insights.quote: it seems unlikely European rearmament will slow down just because of a change in Congress.

insights.claim: Foreign buyers of US munitions like Tomahawk, Patriot and THAAD face uncertainty on delivery timelines because US production ramp-up depends on contested budget packages.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Munitions backlog and pricing stay elevated; ramp-up timing risk for primes and buyers.
